title: SABRE-FL: Selective and Accurate Backdoor Rejection for Federated Prompt Learning
claim: A learnable imperceptible trigger shifts image embeddings away from their true text features, causing targeted misclassification in prompt-learning pipelines.
layout: Single panel, left-to-right data flow, with a feedback loop to the prompt generator
description: A single-panel pipeline diagram of the attack on a CLIP-style prompt learner. At the top left, class-name boxes (elephant, flamingo, dolphin) with animal icons sit above learnable prompt tokens V1..Vn, which are marked with flame icons, plus a CLASS token. These feed a blue trapezoid Text Encoder (frozen, snowflake icon) that outputs colored starburst text features. At the bottom left, an elephant photo is added to a noisy learnable trigger texture to form a poisoned image. That image goes into an orange Image Encoder (also frozen). The resulting image feature, shown as a white star, is compared with the text features in a dark circle for similarity calculation. A red dotted ring marks the mismatch: the actual label is elephant but the predicted label is dolphin. A feedback line runs from the image feature to a Context generator box with a devil icon, which updates the learnable prompts.
caption: Backdoor attack on prompt-learning-based multimodal models. A learnable and imperceptible noise trigger is added to the image that results in a poisoned image embedding, which is then used to generate the learnable prompts. This addition of noise causes the image features to deviate from their respective text features in the embedding space, thereby causing misclassification.
abstract: Federated Prompt Learning has emerged as a communication-efficient and privacy-preserving paradigm for adapting large vision-language models like CLIP across decentralized clients. However, the security implications of this setup remain underexplored. In this work, we present the first study of backdoor attacks in Federated Prompt Learning. We show that when malicious clients inject visually imperceptible, learnable noise triggers into input images, the global prompt learner becomes vulnerable to targeted misclassification while still maintaining high accuracy on clean inputs. Motivated by this vulnerability, we propose SABRE-FL, a lightweight, modular defense that filters poisoned prompt updates using an embedding-space anomaly detector trained offline on out-of-distribution data. SABRE-FL requires no access to raw client data or labels and generalizes across diverse datasets. We show, both theoretically and empirically, that malicious clients can be reliably identified and filtered using an embedding-based detector. Across five diverse datasets and four baseline defenses, SABRE-FL outperforms all baselines by significantly reducing backdoor accuracy while preserving clean accuracy, demonstrating strong empirical performance and underscoring the need for robust prompt learning in future federated systems.
